chapter_theme: Aravanar completes his account of faulty inference for Manimekalai: the inconclusive reasons, the four contradictory reasons (two of them turned against Sankhya and Vaisheshika proofs), and the ten faulty examples, ending with the charge to examine and know true from false without doubt. The teacher's examples mostly defend the rival thesis that sound is eternal, and the whole is the method he gives before the doctrine of kaathai 30.

cast.role: the Buddhist teacher of Puhar, now in Kanchi, who teaches Manimekalai the means of knowledge and the dharma
Madhavi's daughter, a Buddhist renunciant, here Aravanar's pupil

manimekalai:29:234-253.unit_note: Boundary moved from 248 to 253: the second fallacy, defined at 243 to 245, has its example and its closing questions to எனல் at line 253; the core unit broke it at 248.
manimekalai:29:234-253.reading: Aravanar finishes the reason found in some similar cases and in every dissimilar one, with sound said not to arise from effort because it is impermanent (lightning arises without effort, space never shows it, the pot does), then gives its mirror, the reason found in every similar case and some dissimilar ones, with sound said to arise from effort because impermanent.
manimekalai:29:234-253.nuance: The two fallacies are built on one example turned round, which is why each ends in a pair of questions (240 to 242, 251 to 253): 'like the pot, or like the lightning?'. The teacher's point is that an inconclusive reason leaves the hearer with a question, not a verdict.

claims.claim: a reason found in some similar instances and in all dissimilar ones leaves the thesis open to doubt
a reason found in all similar instances and in only some dissimilar ones is likewise inconclusive

manimekalai:29:254-266.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 254 and 266: the fallacy is named at 254 and its example closes with எனல் at 266.
manimekalai:29:254-266.reading: The reason found in only part of the similar and part of the dissimilar cases: sound is eternal because incorporeal, where incorporeality is in space but not the corporeal atom, and in pleasure but not the pot, so the hearer can ask whether sound is eternal like space or impermanent like pleasure.
manimekalai:29:254-266.nuance: Both the eternal atom (259 to 261) and pleasure as incorporeal and passing (262 to 263) are taken as granted for the example; the teacher does not say here whether he holds them.

claims.claim: a reason found in only part of the similar and part of the dissimilar instances is inconclusive

manimekalai:29:267-280.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 267 and 280: the fallacy is defined from 267, and the four kinds of contradiction close with என்ன நான்கு வகையது ஆகும் at 280; the core unit ran on into the first kind.
manimekalai:29:267-280.reading: The last inconclusive reason is the one that admits a contrary reason: 'sound is impermanent because it arises from effort' meets 'sound is eternal because it is heard, like soundness', both proofs stand and both end in doubt; then the contradictory reason is announced in four kinds.
manimekalai:29:267-280.nuance: This is the one fallacy that no single proof shows: it appears only when two arguments meet, so it names the stalemate of a debate hall. சங்கயம் and ஏகாந்தம் அல்ல (274) set doubt against one-sided certainty in borrowed Sanskrit; the eternal-sound proof is a rival's, though no school is named here.

claims.claim: when a thesis and its contrary are each backed by a reason that looks sound, neither is established and both end in doubt
the contradictory reason is of four kinds, by the property or the subject, in its bare form or in its specific character

manimekalai:29:281-302.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 281 and 302: the first kind of contradiction is defined from அத் தன்மச் சொரூப விபரீத சாதனம் at 281, and the second ends with விபரீதம் at 302; the core units broke both mid-sentence.
manimekalai:29:281-302.reading: The contradictory reason proves the opposite of the property ('sound is eternal because it is made', when the made is impermanent) or destroys its intended character: the argument that the eye and other senses serve another because they are aggregates, like beds and seats, proves that other to be composite, like the user of a bed, and so undoes the partless self it set out to prove.
manimekalai:29:281-302.nuance: The text does not name the school at 291 to 302, but the argument from aggregates serving another and the partless self (நிர் அவயவமாயுள்ள ஆன்மா, 299 to 300) are the Sankhya's, whose purusha kaathai 27 describes; the reply turns the Sankhya proof against its own conclusion rather than denying a self outright. Line 296 இந்தியங்களியும் reads as a slip for the senses in the accusative.

claims.claim: a reason that proves the opposite of the property to be proved is contradictory
a reason that undoes the intended specific character of the property to be proved is contradictory
the senses exist for the sake of another, the self, because they are aggregates, as beds and seats are

manimekalai:29:303-325.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 303 and 325: the third kind begins at 303 and the fourth ends with கெடுத்தது in line 325, which also opens the faulty examples (தீய எடுத்துக்காட்டு ஆவன); the core unit broke at 321.
manimekalai:29:303-325.reading: The reason can also undo the subject itself: the argument that existence is not substance, quality or action because it differs from them, like generality and particularity, takes away the common being of all three and leaves existence nothing, turning being into non-being; and the same reason undoes existence's specific character as what gives the notion 'it is'.
manimekalai:29:303-325.nuance: Substance, quality, action, generality and particularity are the Vaisheshika's categories, and பொருளும் குணமும் கருமமும் with உண்மை (310 to 311) repeats the wording of the Vaisheshika's own account at 27:257 to 258; the school is not named here. Lines 321 to 325, on the fourth kind, are compressed, and the sense of கருத்தாவுடைய கிரியையும் குணமும் (322 to 323) is tentative.

claims.claim: a reason that turns the subject itself into its opposite is contradictory
a reason that proves the absence of the subject's specific character is contradictory
existence is neither substance, quality nor action, because it is distinct from the being of each, as generality and particularity are

manimekalai:29:326-339.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 326 and 339: the faulty examples are introduced at 325 to 326 and the two lists of five end with என்ன இவற்றுள் at 339.
manimekalai:29:326-339.reading: Faulty examples are the semblances of the example, of two kinds as the example was: five by similarity (lacking the reason, lacking the property, lacking both, without the connection, with the connection reversed) and five by difference (not excluding the property, not excluding the reason, excluding neither, without the exclusion, with the exclusion reversed).
manimekalai:29:326-339.nuance: The list is a mirror: each failing of a similar example has a counterpart in the dissimilar one, so the teacher can define the second five by reversing the first. Lines 333 to 335 break words across lines (விபரீதான் / னுவயம், திட் / டாந்த), and 336 to 337 are unusually short.

claims.claim: faulty examples are of two kinds, by similarity and by difference, each in five forms

manimekalai:29:340-358.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 340 and 358: the first kind of faulty example is defined at 340, and the second closes with சாத்திய நித்தத்துவம் குறையும் at 358; the core units broke at 356.
manimekalai:29:340-358.reading: An example by similarity may lack the reason (sound is eternal because incorporeal, like the atom, which is eternal but has form) or lack the property to be proved (like cognition, which is incorporeal but passing).
manimekalai:29:340-358.nuance: Both examples defend 'sound is eternal', so the teacher's faulty examples are all on the rival thesis; the eternal, formed atom and the passing cognition (புத்தி) are taken as granted for the lesson.

claims.claim: an example that lacks the reason's property cannot support the proof
an example that lacks the property to be proved cannot support the proof

manimekalai:29:359-372.unit_note: Boundary moved from 357 to 359: line 358 ends the previous kind, and the definition of lacking both begins at 359.
manimekalai:29:359-372.reading: An example may lack both properties, and this is of two kinds, of an existing thing or a non-existent one; of an existing thing: sound is eternal because incorporeal, like a pot, which came into being and has form, so has neither.

claims.claim: an example that lacks both the property to be proved and the reason fails, whether the example exists or not

manimekalai:29:373-384.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 373 and 384: the non-existent kind is defined from 373 and its verdict ends at குறையும் at 384; ananvaya begins at 385.
manimekalai:29:373-384.reading: Of a non-existent thing: sound is impermanent because it has form, like space; for one who says space is unreal it has neither property, and for one who says it is real, space is eternal and formless, so it lacks both for him too.
manimekalai:29:373-384.nuance: The teacher settles nothing about space: the example fails on either view (381 to 384), so the logic can be taught without deciding the ontology the schools dispute. Who holds 'space is unreal' (ஆகாசம் அசத்து) is not said.

claims.claim: an example fails if one party denies it exists, and fails too if, granted, it lacks the properties

manimekalai:29:385-401.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 385 and 401: ananvaya is defined from 385 and the reversed connection ends with விபரீதம் ஆம் at 401; the core units broke at 386 and 398.
manimekalai:29:385-401.reading: Without the connection is to show the reason and property together in a pot without stating 'whatever is made is impermanent'; with the connection reversed is to say 'whatever is impermanent is made', running from the wider to the narrower, which fails because the wider occurs without the narrower.
manimekalai:29:385-401.nuance: The correct rule, கிருத்தம் அது அநித்தம், is the Buddhist teaching that whatever is made passes; the teacher states it only as the model of a well-formed connection, and the reversed form fails because some impermanent things are not made, as the lightning of 238 to 241 showed.

claims.claim: showing two properties together in one instance, without stating the general rule, does not establish the connection
the rule must run from the narrower property to the wider; stated the other way it fails, since the wider occurs without the narrower
whatever is made is impermanent

manimekalai:29:402-423.unit_note: Boundaries moved to 402 and 423: the dissimilar examples begin at 402 and the second kind ends with சாதனமான அமூர்த்தம் மீளாது at 423; the core units broke at 414.
manimekalai:29:402-423.reading: An example by difference may fail to exclude the property (sound is eternal because incorporeal: 'whatever is not eternal is not incorporeal, like the atom', which is eternal and formed) or fail to exclude the reason ('like action', which is incorporeal and passing).
manimekalai:29:402-423.nuance: Action (கன்மம், 418 to 421) is the incorporeal but passing thing here, a category from the Vaisheshika list; it is not karma in the moral sense.

claims.claim: a dissimilar example must lack the property to be proved; one that keeps it fails
a dissimilar example must lack the reason; one that keeps it fails

manimekalai:29:424-449.unit_note: Boundary moved from 426/427 to 424 and 449: the third dissimilar kind is named at 424 and its non-existent case closes with இலையாகும் at 449; avyatireka begins at 450.
manimekalai:29:424-449.reading: An example by difference may exclude neither property, again of an existing or a non-existent thing: for one who holds space a real thing, space is eternal and formless and so excludes neither; for one who says space is no thing, it has no being, so nothing is excluded or kept.
manimekalai:29:424-449.nuance: Space is again judged by both views (437, 446), as at 381 to 384. Line 443 lacks a negative the sense needs (whatever is not impermanent), and 444 has அன்ன்று; the lines read as corrupt.

claims.claim: a dissimilar example from which neither property is excluded fails, whether it exists or not

manimekalai:29:450-472.unit_note: Boundary moved from 456 to 450: avyatireka is defined from 450, and the four closing lines (469 to 472) cannot stand as a unit; the core unit 445-455 broke the definition at 455.
manimekalai:29:450-472.reading: Without the exclusion is to show the pot made and passing without stating that where the property is absent the reason is absent; with the exclusion reversed is to deny the reason before the property; and Aravanar closes by bidding Manimekalai learn by these rules, having examined, to know without doubt what is true and false in the semblances of inference.
manimekalai:29:450-472.nuance: The lesson that began with the true means of knowledge ends with false inference, and its last word is a method for the hearer (ஆய்ந்து அறிந்து கொள்), not a doctrine to accept. Line 463 (என்றால் என்று நின்ற இடத்து) reads awkwardly and may be corrupt.
manimekalai:29:450-472.event: Aravanar ends his account of faulty inference and tells Manimekalai to examine and know true from false by these rules.

claims.claim: the exclusion must be stated as a rule, not only shown in an instance
the exclusion must deny the property to be proved first and the reason after; reversed, it fails
by these rules one can examine an inference and know without doubt what in it is true and what false

links.note: Kaathai 27's Sankhya speaker gives the person as one, pervading and eternal awareness; here the argument for that person from the senses serving another is shown to prove a composite self.
links.teaches: The epic answers the Sankhya two kaathais later without denying it outright: its own proof for a partless self, followed through, yields a self with parts, so the refutation is internal.

links.note: The Vaisheshika says generality gives being (உண்மை) to substance, quality and action; here the argument that being is other than substance, quality and action is shown to make being nothing.
links.teaches: Read together, the units show the Buddhist teacher taking the Vaisheshika's own words for being and showing that its category, argued as the Vaisheshika argues it, empties itself.

links.note: The Vaisheshika counts space among the nine substances; the teacher judges examples built on space under both views, that it is a thing and that it is not.
links.teaches: The pairing shows the logic lesson deliberately leaving the schools' quarrel over space unsettled: a proof is faulted on either view, so the method does not depend on deciding the rival's ontology.

links.note: The Vedic logician lists eight false semblances of knowledge, errors of seeing and remembering; the Buddhist teacher ends with the semblances of inference, errors in a stated proof.
links.teaches: The two catalogues of error divide the ground differently: the logician locates falsehood in a mistaken cognition, the Buddhist teacher in a badly built argument, which can be checked rule by rule.

links.note: The Kural says that a mind which examines (ஓர்த்து) and knows what is with certainty (ஒருதலையா) need not think of birth again; Aravanar closes with examine (ஆய்ந்து) and know without doubt (ஐயம் இன்றி).
links.teaches: The couplet names examination and certainty as the way out of birth but gives no procedure; the epic supplies one, and its technical word for certainty, ஏகாந்தம், is the couplet's ஒருதலை in Sanskrit dress.

gains.a: the fallacy list gains a stated end beyond winning debates, the certainty the Kural ties to release
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'examine and be certain' gains tests for when an argument has earned certainty

links.note: Tirumular says the wise gave up logic and disputation (தர்க்க வாதம்) and gained release by reciting the Veda; Aravanar, who folds scripture into inference, ends his teaching of dharma with the rules of disputation.
links.teaches: The two give opposite answers to whether argument leads toward release: for Tirumular it is what the wise leave behind, for the Buddhist teacher it is the discipline that sorts true from false before doctrine is heard.

gains.a: the epic's logic lesson gains a named Saiva rejection of the very method it teaches
gains.b: Tirumular's dismissal of argument gains a full example of the argument he dismisses, from a school that grants the Veda no separate authority

links.note: The Kural promises the sky to those who have left doubt and become clear; the teacher describes two sound-looking proofs of opposite theses that together leave only doubt (சங்கயம்).
links.teaches: The epic shows a doubt that more argument cannot remove, since each side's reasoning holds, so the clarity the couplet praises cannot come from matching proofs alone.

gains.a: the stalemate fallacy gains its stake: doubt is what the Kural says bars the way to the sky
gains.b: the couplet's 'leaving doubt' gains a precise case of doubt that reasoning itself produces

links.note: The Kural calls taking what does not last for what lasts the lowest understanding; Aravanar's model rule is 'whatever is made is impermanent', valid only in that direction.
links.teaches: Set beside the couplet, the textbook rule shows impermanence as something proved from being made, with the warning that the converse fails, so knowing the passing is a matter of inference as well as of seeing.

gains.a: the stock example gains the moral weight the Kural gives to knowing impermanence
gains.b: the couplet's demand to see the passing as passing gains a stated form of proof and its limit

links.note: Arunagirinathar lumps Buddhists with the followers of Kapila and Kanada as clamouring disputants whose books cannot give the teaching; here a Buddhist teacher takes apart arguments of the Sankhya and the Vaisheshika by formal logic.
links.teaches: The pair shows the same quarrel from inside and outside: what the devotee hears as noise of books, the epic presents as a disciplined refutation, and it is the Buddhist the devotee counts first among the noisy.

gains.a: the epic's refutation gains a later Saiva verdict that its whole contest misses the point
gains.b: the song's list of disputants gains a working example of how those schools actually argued against each other

new_concepts.gloss: a false semblance in inference: a thesis, reason or example that looks like part of a sound proof but fails (also போலி)
new_concepts.label_source: The text's word: திட்டாந்த ஆபாசங்கள் (326), திட்டாந்த ஆபாசம் (329, 334 to 335), அனுமான ஆபாசம் (470)

source_issues: manimekalai:29 line 296: இந்தியங்களியும் reads as a slip for the senses in the accusative (இந்திரியங்களையும்); 298 has இந்தியத்துக்கும் for the same word.
manimekalai:29 lines 333 to 335: words are broken across lines (விபரீதான் / னுவயம், திட் / டாந்த), and 336 to 337, 345 and 354 are very short lines.
manimekalai:29 lines 443 to 444: the dissimilar example lacks the negation the sense needs after அநித்தம், and 444 has the misprint அன்ன்று.
manimekalai:29 line 463: என்றால் என்று நின்ற இடத்து reads awkwardly and may be corrupt.
manimekalai:29 lines 234 to 472: most core unit boundaries fall mid-definition (break score 0 or 1); thirteen adjusted units follow the fallacy definitions.
